courses.title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals
courses.short_description: Understand how public cloud actually works, from regions and virtual machines to cost and security.
courses.description:
Most cloud courses start with a console tour. This one starts with the problems cloud was built to solve, because service names change and the underlying reasoning does not.

You will learn how physical infrastructure is abstracted into regions and availability zones, why the shared responsibility model determines who is accountable when something breaks, how the main compute and storage options differ in ways that matter, and how consumption pricing turns architecture decisions into monthly costs.

By the end you will be able to read a cloud architecture diagram, explain why each component is there, and estimate roughly what it costs to run.
learning_outcomes: Explain regions, availability zones and how they affect resilience
Apply the shared responsibility model to decide who secures what
Choose between virtual machines, containers and serverless for a given workload
Select an appropriate storage class from access pattern and durability needs
Estimate the running cost of a simple architecture
Describe how identity and access management prevents over-permissioning
requirements: No programming or infrastructure experience required

modules.title: What cloud computing actually is
modules.description: The problems public cloud solves, and the vocabulary used to describe it.

lessons.title: Why cloud replaced buying servers
lessons.content:
## The problem with owning hardware

Before public cloud, capacity was a purchasing decision made months ahead of demand. You estimated peak load, bought hardware to match, and then owned that peak capacity permanently -- paying for it during the 95% of the time you did not need it, and still being short during the 5% you underestimated.

That produced two failure modes that shaped everything cloud does:

- **Over-provisioning.** Money spent on idle capacity, plus the operational burden of maintaining machines that mostly wait.
- **Under-provisioning.** Demand arrives, capacity does not, and the lead time to add more is measured in weeks.

## What changed

Public cloud converts that capital purchase into a usage charge. Capacity becomes something you request in seconds and release when you are done, and you pay for what you consumed.

This has three consequences worth internalising early:

1. **Architecture became an economic decision.** Choosing a larger instance is no longer a procurement request; it is a line item that recurs monthly. Engineers now make cost decisions whether or not they realise it.
2. **Failure became something you design around, not prevent.** When capacity is disposable, the correct response to a failed machine is to replace it, not repair it.
3. **Speed of iteration went up.** Trying an idea costs an afternoon rather than a purchase order.

## What did not change

Cloud does not remove the need to understand networking, storage characteristics or security. It changes who operates the hardware, not whether those concepts matter. The rest of this course covers the parts that still require your judgement.

lessons.title: Service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
lessons.content:
## A single question separates the three

*How much of the stack do you still operate?*

### Infrastructure as a service
You get virtual machines, disks and networks. The provider runs the physical hardware and hypervisor; you run the operating system upward -- patching, configuration, and everything installed on it. Maximum control, maximum operational work.

### Platform as a service
You get a managed runtime: you supply the application, the provider runs the operating system, patching and scaling. You give up the ability to install arbitrary system software in exchange for not maintaining any.

### Software as a service
You get a finished application. You configure it and manage your data inside it; you operate none of it.

## How to choose in practice

The honest default is: **use the most managed option that meets your requirements.** Every layer you take on is a layer you must patch, monitor and staff.

Move down the stack only when something forces you to -- a specific kernel version, a licensing constraint, a network topology the managed service cannot express, or a cost profile that only works with reserved capacity you manage yourself.

## The trap

Teams often choose infrastructure as a service because it feels safer or more flexible, then discover they have signed up for permanent operational work they never budgeted for. Flexibility you do not use is pure cost.

lessons.title: Regions, availability zones and edge locations
lessons.content:
## The physical reality underneath

A **region** is a geographic area -- roughly, a metropolitan area -- containing multiple isolated groups of data centres. Regions are far apart, so a disaster affecting one does not affect another. They are also independently priced, and network traffic between them costs money and takes time.

An **availability zone** is one or more discrete data centres within a region, with independent power, cooling and networking. Zones within a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but isolated enough that a power failure or flood in one does not take down another.

An **edge location** is a smaller facility used for caching content closer to users than the region is.

## Why this determines your architecture

Three design decisions follow directly:

1. **Which region.** Driven by where your users are (latency), where your data is legally allowed to live (residency), and price -- regions do not cost the same.
2. **How many zones.** A single-zone deployment fails when that zone fails. Spreading across zones is the cheapest meaningful resilience you can buy, and it is usually a configuration change rather than an architectural one.
3. **Whether to span regions.** Multi-region is significantly more expensive and complex. It is justified by a recovery objective that a single region cannot meet, or by users far enough away that latency hurts -- not by a general wish for reliability.

## A rule of thumb

Multi-zone by default. Multi-region only when a written requirement forces it.

modules.title: Core services and how to choose between them
modules.description: Compute, storage and networking, framed as decisions rather than feature lists.

lessons.title: Compute: virtual machines, containers and serverless
lessons.content:
## The three models

**Virtual machines** give you a whole operating system. You control everything and you maintain everything. Best when you need specific system-level software, long-running processes, or predictable steady load where reserved pricing pays off.

**Containers** package an application with its dependencies and run it on shared infrastructure. You control the application environment but not the host. Best for services that scale horizontally and are deployed frequently.

**Serverless functions** run your code in response to events and charge per invocation. You control nothing but the code. Best for bursty, event-driven work with idle periods.

## The decision, honestly

Ask three questions:

1. **What is the unit of work?** A request, a batch job, or a process that must stay resident? Resident processes rule out functions immediately.
2. **How spiky is demand?** Deeply spiky, with long idle periods, favours per-invocation pricing. Steady load favours reserved capacity.
3. **What can the team operate?** A container platform that nobody on the team understands is not the cheaper option regardless of the pricing page.

## The constraints that decide it

Some constraints eliminate options outright, and these are worth memorising:

- Execution time limits eliminate serverless functions for long-running jobs.
- Cold-start latency eliminates serverless for latency-critical synchronous paths unless you pay to keep instances warm.
- Specific OS or kernel requirements eliminate managed container platforms.
- Licensing tied to physical cores can eliminate shared infrastructure entirely.

When an exam question or a design review presents four workable options, one of these constraints is usually what makes three of them wrong.

lessons.title: Storage: objects, blocks and files
lessons.content:
## Three shapes of storage

**Object storage** holds whole files addressed by a key, reachable over HTTP, effectively unlimited in size, and extremely durable. It cannot be mounted as a filesystem and you cannot modify part of an object in place. Use it for uploads, backups, static assets and data lakes.

**Block storage** is a virtual disk attached to one machine. It behaves like a physical drive: format it, mount it, write to it at the block level. Use it for databases and operating system disks.

**File storage** is a shared filesystem multiple machines can mount at once. More expensive per gigabyte, but the only option when several machines genuinely need the same mutable filesystem.

## Storage classes and the cost trap

Within object storage there are classes trading retrieval cost against storage cost. Colder classes are dramatically cheaper to store and progressively more expensive -- and slower -- to read.

The trap: colder classes usually carry a **minimum storage duration**. Moving objects to an archive class and then deleting or reading them a week later can cost more than leaving them in the standard class. Lifecycle rules should reflect real access patterns, not an assumption that colder is always cheaper.

## Choosing

- Does more than one machine need to write to it simultaneously? -> file storage.
- Does something need to treat it as a disk? -> block storage.
- Otherwise -> object storage, and pick the class from how often it is actually read.

lessons.title: Networking and the shared responsibility model
lessons.content:
## Private networks in the cloud

Your resources live inside a virtual network with an address range you choose, divided into subnets. Two rules matter more than the rest:

1. **Address ranges must not overlap** with anything you may later need to connect to. Overlapping ranges make peering to another network or to on-premises impossible without renumbering, which is far more painful than planning generously up front.
2. **Subnets are usually the unit of security policy.** Group resources by trust boundary rather than by application tier for its own sake.

Anything that must not be reachable from the internet should have no public address at all -- a firewall rule you can misconfigure is weaker than an address that does not exist.

## The shared responsibility model

This is the single most useful mental model in cloud security, and it appears on every foundational exam.

**The provider secures the cloud itself:** physical facilities, hardware, the hypervisor, and the managed service internals.

**You secure what you put in it:** your data, who can access it, how your network is configured, how your application is written, and how your credentials are handled.

The line moves depending on the service model. On a virtual machine, operating-system patching is yours. On a managed database, it is the provider's -- but the database user permissions are still yours.

## Why breaches happen

Almost never because the provider's infrastructure failed. Overwhelmingly because of the customer side of that line: a storage bucket left publicly readable, an over-permissive role, a credential committed to a repository. Understanding which side of the line a task falls on is most of practical cloud security.

modules.title: Cost, identity and putting it together
modules.description: The two topics that decide whether a cloud deployment is sustainable.

lessons.title: How cloud pricing actually works
lessons.content:
## Four things you pay for

1. **Compute time** - per second or hour, varying by size. Usually the largest line item.
2. **Storage** - per gigabyte-month, varying by class and redundancy.
3. **Data transfer** - inbound is typically free; outbound to the internet and between regions is not. This is the line that surprises people.
4. **Requests and operations** - per-API-call charges on storage and serverless services.

## Pricing models

- **On demand** - no commitment, highest unit price. Correct for unpredictable or short-lived work.
- **Committed or reserved** - one to three year commitment for a substantial discount. Correct for steady baseline load you are confident will persist.
- **Spot or preemptible** - deeply discounted spare capacity that can be reclaimed with little notice. Correct for interruptible batch work, wrong for anything a user is waiting on.

A common production pattern is reserved capacity for the baseline, on-demand for normal variation, spot for batch.

## Estimating before you build

Before deploying anything, write down: how many instances of what size, running how many hours; how many gigabytes stored in which class; and roughly how much data leaves the network each month. Multiply by the published rates. You will not be exact, but you will be within the right order of magnitude -- which is enough to catch a design that is unaffordable before you build it.

## Where costs actually run away

Idle non-production environments, forgotten storage that nothing reads, over-sized instances chosen defensively, and cross-region data transfer added without anyone modelling the volume.

lessons.title: Identity and access management
lessons.content:
## The model

Every cloud platform expresses access the same way: a **principal** (a person, a group, or a workload identity) is granted a **role** (a bundle of permitted actions) at a **scope** (the set of resources it applies to).

Get those three right and most access problems disappear.

## Least privilege, concretely

Grant the narrowest role that covers the actions needed, at the narrowest scope that covers the resources needed. Broad grants at broad scopes are the single most common cloud misconfiguration, and they are usually made for convenience during setup and never revisited.

A practical test: if you cannot name the specific task that requires a permission, remove it and wait for something to break. Something breaking is cheap; a compromised over-permissioned credential is not.

## Workload identity beats keys

Applications need to authenticate too. The wrong way is a long-lived access key stored in a config file, because it will eventually be committed to a repository, shared in a chat message, or left behind on a decommissioned machine.

The right way is an identity attached to the compute resource itself, from which short-lived credentials are issued automatically. Nothing to store, nothing to leak, nothing to rotate manually.

## Groups, not individuals

Assign roles to groups and manage membership. Per-person assignments become impossible to audit within a year, and the audit is the point.

lessons.title: Design exercise: a small production system
lessons.content:
## The brief

Design the infrastructure for a web application with a database. Requirements:

- Roughly 5,000 daily users, concentrated in one country.
- Must survive the loss of a single data centre.
- User-uploaded images, retained indefinitely but rarely re-read after 60 days.
- Data must remain within the country.
- Modest budget; the team is three engineers with no dedicated operations staff.

## Work it through before reading on

Write down the constraints and what each one eliminates.

## Reference reasoning

**Region.** Data residency decides it -- a region inside the country, not the cheapest region available. This constraint alone eliminates most options.

**Zones.** "Survive the loss of a single data centre" means multi-zone within that region. It does *not* mean multi-region; adding a second region here would satisfy the requirement while badly overshooting the budget, which makes it the wrong answer.

**Compute.** A team of three with no operations staff points to a managed platform rather than self-managed virtual machines. Traffic at this scale is modest and steady, so serverless per-invocation pricing offers little advantage over a small always-on managed service.

**Database.** A managed relational database with a standby in a second zone. Automated backups and patching are handled, which matters more than the price difference at this team size.

**Images.** Object storage with a lifecycle rule moving objects to a cooler class after 60 days -- matching the stated access pattern, not an assumption that colder is always better.

**Networking.** The database has no public address. The application reaches it privately.

**Identity.** A workload identity on the application for storage and database access; no static keys anywhere.

## The point

Every decision traced back to a stated constraint. When you cannot name the constraint driving a choice, you are guessing -- and that is exactly what both design reviews and certification exams are testing for.

courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
courses.short_description: What modern AI systems can and cannot do, how they are built, and how to evaluate them honestly.
courses.description:
A conceptual introduction for people who need to reason about AI systems rather than train them from scratch.

The course covers what distinguishes machine learning from traditional software, how neural networks and language models actually produce output, where these systems reliably fail, and how to evaluate a claim about an AI system's performance without taking the claim on faith.

There is no advanced mathematics. There is a lot of emphasis on evaluation, because the difference between a useful AI system and an impressive demonstration is almost always measurement.
learning_outcomes: Explain how machine learning differs from rule-based software
Describe at a conceptual level how neural networks and language models work
Identify common failure modes including hallucination and distribution shift
Evaluate an AI claim using appropriate metrics rather than accuracy alone
Recognise where bias enters a machine learning pipeline
Decide when a problem is a poor fit for machine learning
requirements: Comfort with basic statistics is helpful but not required

modules.title: What AI is, precisely
modules.description: Separating the field from the marketing.

lessons.title: Rules versus learned behaviour
lessons.content:
## Traditional software

A developer writes rules. The rules are inspected, tested and, when wrong, corrected in a specific place. Behaviour is a direct consequence of instructions someone wrote deliberately.

## Machine learning

You supply examples of inputs and desired outputs, and an algorithm searches for a function that maps between them. Nobody writes the rule. The rule is discovered, encoded as numbers, and is generally not interpretable by reading it.

## The trade you are making

Machine learning is worth it when the rules are genuinely hard to write down. Nobody can specify in code what makes an image contain a cat; a model can learn it from examples.

But you give up three things:

1. **Inspectability.** You cannot read the model to find out why it made a decision.
2. **Predictability on new inputs.** The model behaves well on data resembling its training data, and its behaviour outside that distribution is not guaranteed.
3. **Determinism about correctness.** You cannot prove the model is right; you can only measure how often it is right on data you have.

## When not to use machine learning

If the rule can be written down, write it down. A regular expression that validates an email format is better than a model that classifies email addresses: it is faster, free, auditable, and correct by construction. Reaching for a model where a rule suffices adds cost, latency and an entire class of failure modes for no benefit.

lessons.title: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning
lessons.content:
## Supervised learning

You have inputs paired with correct answers. The model learns to predict the answer. This covers the large majority of deployed machine learning: classification (which category?) and regression (what value?).

The binding constraint is labelled data. Labels are expensive, and label quality caps model quality -- a model trained on inconsistently labelled data learns the inconsistency.

## Unsupervised learning

You have inputs with no answers, and you want structure: clusters of similar items, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection.

The difficulty is evaluation. With no ground truth, "good" is a judgement call, and clustering results can look meaningful while being an artefact of the distance metric you chose.

## Reinforcement learning

An agent takes actions in an environment and receives rewards. It learns a policy that maximises cumulative reward.

Powerful in simulation, difficult in the physical world, because it learns by trying things -- and in a real environment, trying things has consequences. It also optimises exactly what you reward, which is rarely exactly what you meant.

## Choosing

- Do you have labelled examples of what you want predicted? -> supervised.
- Do you want to find structure you cannot describe in advance? -> unsupervised.
- Are you optimising a sequence of decisions with delayed feedback? -> reinforcement.

Most business problems that appear to need reinforcement learning are better served by supervised learning plus explicit rules.

lessons.title: How neural networks learn
lessons.content:
## The structure

A neural network is layers of simple units. Each unit multiplies its inputs by weights, sums them, adds a bias and applies a non-linear function. Stack enough layers and the network can approximate very complex mappings.

The non-linearity is essential: without it, any stack of layers collapses mathematically into a single linear layer, and the depth buys nothing.

## Training, in four steps

1. **Forward pass.** Push an input through and get a prediction.
2. **Loss.** Compute a number measuring how wrong it was.
3. **Backward pass.** Compute, for every weight, the direction that would reduce the loss.
4. **Update.** Nudge every weight slightly in that direction.

Repeat millions of times. That is the entire algorithm. There is no reasoning step and no comprehension; there is iterative error reduction.

## Overfitting: the central problem

A model with enough capacity can memorise its training data, achieving near-perfect training accuracy while performing badly on anything new. It has learned the specific examples rather than the pattern.

This is why you always hold out data the model never sees during training. **Training accuracy is not evidence of anything.** A model reported without a held-out evaluation set should be treated as unevaluated.

## Why more data usually beats a cleverer model

More, cleaner, more representative data reduces overfitting directly and improves behaviour on inputs the model has not seen. In practice, teams reach for architectural sophistication when they should be fixing their data.

modules.title: Language models and where they fail
modules.description: How large language models produce text, and the failure modes that follow from it.

lessons.title: How language models generate text
lessons.content:
## Next-token prediction

A language model is trained on one task: given a sequence of text, predict what comes next. Text is broken into tokens -- roughly word fragments -- and the model outputs a probability distribution over the possible next token. One is selected, appended, and the process repeats.

Everything the model appears to do emerges from this. It has no separate module for reasoning, facts or intent. Coherent argument and factual recall are both consequences of predicting plausible continuations of text.

## Why attention mattered

Earlier architectures processed text sequentially and struggled to connect distant words. Attention lets every token be weighted against every other token directly, so a pronoun can be linked to a noun many sentences earlier. That change, plus scale, produced the current generation of models.

## What follows from the training objective

Three consequences are worth stating plainly:

1. **Plausibility is the objective, not truth.** The model produces text that looks like a good continuation. Accurate text is usually plausible, which is why it is often right -- but plausibility is what is being optimised.
2. **Knowledge has a cutoff.** Anything after training is unknown unless supplied in the prompt.
3. **There is no internal fact-check.** Nothing compares the output against a source of truth unless you build that step yourself.

## Practical implication

A language model is an excellent tool for transforming text you supply and a fundamentally unreliable one for recalling facts you did not supply. Systems that give the model its sources and ask it to work from them are far more reliable than systems that rely on what the model absorbed during training.

lessons.title: Hallucination, bias and distribution shift
lessons.content:
## Hallucination

A model states something false with the same fluency as something true. This is not a bug that will be patched away -- it follows directly from optimising for plausible continuations. A fabricated citation is plausible-looking text; that is precisely what the model was trained to produce.

Mitigations that actually help: supply the source material in the prompt, require citations that can be checked programmatically, and constrain the output format. Mitigations that do not help: instructing the model not to hallucinate.

## Bias

Bias enters at four points, and only the last is about the algorithm:

1. **Sampling.** Who is represented in the training data, and who is not.
2. **Labelling.** Human annotators bring their own assumptions.
3. **Objective.** What you chose to optimise encodes a value judgement.
4. **Deployment.** A model performing acceptably on average can perform badly for a specific group.

This is why aggregate accuracy is insufficient. Performance must be measured per relevant subgroup, or you will ship something that works well overall and fails a minority of users consistently.

## Distribution shift

Models degrade when live data drifts away from training data -- and it always drifts, because the world changes. A model trained on last year's user behaviour is describing last year.

The practical requirement is monitoring: track input distributions and output distributions in production, and alert on change. A model with no monitoring is a model whose current accuracy nobody knows.

lessons.title: Evaluating an AI claim
lessons.content:
## Accuracy is usually the wrong number

Consider a fraud detector on a dataset where 1% of transactions are fraudulent. A model that labels everything as legitimate is 99% accurate and completely worthless.

Whenever classes are imbalanced -- which is most interesting problems -- accuracy hides the failure.

## The metrics that carry information

- **Precision** - of the items flagged, what fraction were correct? Low precision means false alarms.
- **Recall** - of the items that should have been flagged, what fraction were? Low recall means misses.
- **F1** - the harmonic mean of the two, useful as a single summary.

Precision and recall trade against each other. Which one you favour is a business decision, not a technical one: a cancer screen should favour recall and accept false alarms; a spam filter should favour precision and accept some spam getting through, because deleting real mail is worse.

## Questions to ask about any AI claim

1. **Measured on what data?** Held-out data the model never saw, or training data?
2. **Which metric, and why that one?**
3. **Compared against what baseline?** A model must beat the simplest reasonable alternative -- often a handful of rules -- or it is not earning its complexity.
4. **How does it perform per subgroup**, not just on average?
5. **When was it last evaluated on current production data?**

A claim that survives all five is credible. Most published claims do not survive the first.

modules.title: Applying AI responsibly
modules.description: Deciding when to use these systems, and how to deploy them without causing harm.

lessons.title: Deciding whether to use machine learning at all
lessons.content:
## Four questions before you start

1. **Can the rule be written down?** If yes, write it. Rules are cheaper, faster, auditable and correct by construction.
2. **Do you have enough representative data?** Not just volume -- representativeness. Data from one region, one season or one customer segment produces a model that works only there.
3. **What does being wrong cost?** A recommendation that misses is a minor annoyance. A loan decision that misses is a serious harm to a person and a legal exposure to you. The cost of error determines how much evaluation and human oversight the system needs.
4. **Can you tell whether it is working in production?** If you cannot measure quality after deployment, you cannot operate the system responsibly -- you can only hope.

## Problems that are a poor fit

- Rare events with almost no positive examples.
- Domains where the underlying relationship changes faster than you can retrain.
- Decisions that legally require an explanation you cannot produce.
- Anything where a simple rule already performs acceptably.

## The honest default

Start with the simplest thing that could work -- often rules, or a basic statistical model -- and measure it. That baseline tells you whether a more complex model is worth its cost. Teams that skip the baseline routinely deploy expensive models that beat nothing.

lessons.title: Humans in the loop, and where to place them
lessons.content:
## Three patterns

**Human in the loop.** Every decision is reviewed by a person before it takes effect. Highest safety, lowest throughput. Correct for high-stakes, low-volume decisions -- medical, legal, financial.

**Human on the loop.** The system acts automatically; people monitor and can intervene. Correct for moderate stakes at volume, provided the monitoring is real rather than nominal.

**Human out of the loop.** Fully automatic. Only defensible when errors are cheap and reversible.

## Placing the human where it helps

Reviewing everything is expensive and produces rubber-stamping: a reviewer who approves 500 correct decisions in a row stops reading the 501st.

Better is to route by model confidence -- automate the confident majority and send genuinely uncertain cases to a person. This concentrates human attention where it changes the outcome. It requires calibrated confidence scores, which are worth building for that reason alone.

## Recourse

Anyone affected by an automated decision needs a way to contest it, and someone with authority to reverse it. This is increasingly a legal requirement, and it is the right design regardless. A system with no appeal path is a system whose errors are permanent.

lessons.title: Course review and where to go next
lessons.content:
## What you should now be able to do

- Explain why a learned rule differs fundamentally from a written one, and what you trade for it.
- Describe how a neural network is trained and why held-out evaluation is non-negotiable.
- Explain how a language model produces text, and why hallucination follows from that mechanism.
- Pick an appropriate metric for a problem and challenge a claim measured with the wrong one.
- Name where bias enters a pipeline, and why aggregate accuracy hides subgroup failure.
- Decide when a problem should not be solved with machine learning.

## Where to go from here

If you want to build models, the next step is a machine learning course covering the actual workflow: data preparation, model selection, validation strategy and deployment.

If you want to work with data more broadly, a data science course covering statistics, SQL and visualisation gives you the foundation that machine learning sits on.

If your role is to evaluate or govern AI systems rather than build them, you already have most of what you need. The highest-value next step is practice: take three AI claims from vendors or papers and run each through the five evaluation questions from module two.

courses.short_description: The end-to-end machine learning workflow: data preparation, model selection, validation and deployment.
courses.description:
A practical course on the workflow that surrounds a model, because the model is rarely the hard part.

You will work through framing a problem, preparing and splitting data without leaking information, choosing between model families, validating honestly, and the operational realities of running a model in production -- monitoring, drift and retraining.

Examples use Python and scikit-learn conventions, but the reasoning transfers to any toolkit.

Choose a validation strategy appropriate to the data structure
Select between linear models, tree ensembles and neural networks with reasons
Diagnose underfitting and overfitting from learning curves

modules.title: Framing and preparing
modules.description: The decisions made before any model is trained, which determine whether the project can succeed.

lessons.title: Turning a business problem into an ML problem
lessons.content:
## Most failures happen here

A project that is framed badly cannot be rescued by a better model. Framing means answering four questions precisely.

### 1. What exactly is being predicted?

"Predict customer churn" is not a specification. "Predict whether an account with an active subscription today will have cancelled 30 days from now" is. The second version tells you what a row is, what the label is, and when it is known.

### 2. What is available at prediction time?

This is the question that kills projects late. If a feature is only recorded after the event you are predicting, it cannot be used -- however predictive it looks in the training data. A cancellation-reason field predicts churn perfectly and is worthless, because it exists only after churn.

### 3. What is the decision this prediction changes?

If no action follows from the prediction, the model has no value regardless of accuracy. Name the action first, then work backwards to the prediction that would inform it, and to the metric that reflects whether the action improved.

### 4. What does a mistake cost, in each direction?

False positives and false negatives almost never cost the same. Retention offers sent to customers who would have stayed cost you a discount; missed churners cost a customer. That ratio determines your decision threshold, and it is a business input, not a technical one.

## Write it down

A one-page framing document -- prediction target, prediction time, available features, decision, cost of each error type, and success metric -- takes an hour and prevents most of the ways these projects fail.

lessons.title: Data preparation and leakage
lessons.content:
## Leakage: the most expensive bug in machine learning

Leakage is any situation where information reaches the model that would not be available at prediction time. It produces excellent validation scores and a model that fails immediately in production, and it is often discovered only after deployment.

### Target leakage

A feature encodes the answer. The cancellation-reason field for churn. A `discount_applied` flag that is only ever set for converted customers.

**Test:** for every feature, ask when its value is written relative to the event being predicted. Anything written after is leakage.

### Train/test contamination

You compute a transformation -- scaling, imputation, encoding -- over the whole dataset and then split. The training set now carries information about the test set.

**Fix:** split first. Fit every transformation on the training set only, then apply it to validation and test. A pipeline object that bundles preprocessing with the model makes this the default rather than a discipline you have to remember.

### Temporal leakage

Randomly splitting time-ordered data lets the model train on the future and be evaluated on the past. Every score is meaningless.

**Fix:** for any data with a time dimension, split chronologically. Train on earlier, validate on later. Always.

### Group leakage

The same entity appears in both training and test sets -- multiple visits from one patient, several sessions from one user. The model memorises the entity rather than learning the pattern.

**Fix:** split by group, so all records for an entity land on one side.

## Missing values

Before imputing, ask *why* the value is missing. Missing because a sensor failed is different from missing because the question does not apply. The second case often means the missingness itself is informative -- add an indicator column rather than silently filling in a median and destroying the signal.

lessons.title: Feature engineering that earns its keep
lessons.content:
## What features are for

A model can only use relationships expressible in the representation you give it. Feature engineering is making the useful structure visible.

## Techniques that consistently pay off

**Ratios and differences.** Absolute values are often less informative than relative ones. `spend_this_month / average_monthly_spend` captures a change that raw spend does not.

**Time deltas.** `days_since_last_login` is nearly always more useful than a raw timestamp, because the model does not have to learn the relationship to "now".

**Aggregations over windows.** Count, mean and variance of a behaviour over 7, 30 and 90 days lets the model see both recent state and trend.

**Sensible categorical encoding.** One-hot for low cardinality. For high cardinality, target encoding works but leaks badly if computed outside the training fold -- it must be fitted inside cross-validation, not before it.

## What usually does not pay off

Automatically generating hundreds of polynomial interactions. This inflates dimensionality, increases overfitting risk, and destroys interpretability, usually for a negligible gain. Domain knowledge that suggests one specific interaction beats brute force reliably.

## The discipline

Add features in small batches and measure. A feature that does not improve validation performance is not free -- it costs computation, adds a pipeline dependency that can break, and gives the model another opportunity to overfit.

modules.title: Modelling and validation
modules.description: Choosing a model family and measuring performance in a way you can trust.

lessons.title: Choosing a model family
lessons.content:
## Start with a baseline

Before any model, establish what trivial performance looks like: predict the majority class, or predict the mean. Every subsequent result is measured against that. Without it you cannot tell whether 82% accuracy is impressive or embarrassing.

## Linear and logistic regression

Fast, interpretable, hard to overfit with regularisation, and a genuinely strong baseline on tabular data with mostly linear relationships. Coefficients are directly explainable, which matters when a decision must be justified.

Use when interpretability is required, when data is limited, or as the baseline you must beat.

## Tree ensembles

Gradient-boosted trees and random forests are the practical default for tabular data. They handle non-linearity and interactions without manual engineering, tolerate mixed feature types, need no scaling, and are relatively robust to outliers.

They are usually the right answer for structured business data, and they win most tabular competitions for good reason.

## Neural networks

Dominant for unstructured data -- images, audio, text -- where the network learns the representation itself. On tabular data they typically match rather than beat a well-tuned gradient boosting model while costing far more to train and operate.

Use for unstructured inputs, very large datasets, or when transfer learning from a pretrained model gives you a large head start.

## An honest default

Tabular data: baseline, then gradient boosting, then consider anything else only if that is insufficient. Unstructured data: a pretrained network fine-tuned on your data. Deviating from this needs a reason you can state.

lessons.title: Validation strategy
lessons.content:
## The purpose

Validation estimates performance on data the model has never seen. Every choice below exists to keep that estimate honest.

## Three-way split

- **Training set** - the model learns from this.
- **Validation set** - you compare models and tune hyperparameters against this.
- **Test set** - you touch this once, at the end.

The test set is separate from validation because repeatedly tuning against the validation set gradually overfits to it. After fifty experiments, your validation score is optimistic. The test set is the only unbiased number you have, and checking it twice destroys that property.

## Cross-validation

With limited data, k-fold cross-validation uses all of it: split into k parts, train on k-1 and validate on the remainder, rotate, average. More reliable than a single split, at k times the compute.

**Stratified** k-fold preserves class proportions in each fold, and should be the default for classification with imbalance.

## Time series

Standard cross-validation is invalid on time-ordered data. Use forward chaining: train on the first n periods, validate on n+1; expand and repeat. This mirrors how the model will actually be used -- predicting forward from history.

## Grouped data

If records cluster by entity, use grouped splitting so an entity never appears on both sides. Otherwise you are measuring memorisation.

## Diagnosing from learning curves

Plot training and validation error against training set size.

- **Both high, converged** -> underfitting. The model is too simple, or the features lack signal. More data will not help.
- **Training low, validation high, large gap** -> overfitting. More data, stronger regularisation, or a simpler model will help.
- **Both low and close** -> working. Consider whether more capacity buys anything.

lessons.title: Metrics and thresholds
lessons.content:
## Classification

Accuracy is misleading under class imbalance -- always. Use:

- **Precision** - correctness of positive predictions.
- **Recall** - coverage of actual positives.
- **F1** - harmonic mean, for a single summary.
- **ROC AUC** - ranking quality across all thresholds; can look flattering on heavily imbalanced data.
- **PR AUC** - precision-recall area, more informative when positives are rare.

## The threshold is a business decision

A classifier outputs a probability. Converting it to a decision requires a threshold, and 0.5 is a default, not an answer.

Set the threshold from the relative cost of the two error types. If a false negative costs ten times a false positive, lower the threshold until the ratio of errors reflects that. Do this deliberately with the people who own the cost, and revisit it when the costs change.

## Calibration

If your system uses the probability itself -- routing uncertain cases to humans, or feeding an expected-value calculation -- the probabilities must be calibrated: among cases predicted at 0.7, about 70% should be positive.

Many models, especially boosted trees, are poorly calibrated by default. Check with a calibration plot and correct it if the probability values matter. If you only use the ranking, calibration is irrelevant.

## Regression

- **MAE** - average absolute error, in the units of the target, robust to outliers.
- **RMSE** - penalises large errors more heavily; use when big misses are disproportionately costly.
- **MAPE** - percentage error, useful across different scales, but undefined and unstable near zero.

Report the one that matches how the prediction is used, and report it against the baseline.

modules.title: Deployment and operations
modules.description: What happens after the model works on your machine.

lessons.title: Serving a model
lessons.content:
## Two serving patterns

**Batch.** Predictions are computed on a schedule and written to a store the application reads. Simple, cheap, easy to monitor, and correct whenever predictions do not need to reflect events from the last few minutes.

**Online.** The model is behind an API and predicts per request. Necessary when the input only exists at request time. Brings latency budgets, availability requirements and scaling concerns.

Start with batch unless a requirement forces online. A surprising share of production models never needed real-time serving.

## Training/serving skew

The most common production failure: features computed one way during training and another way at serving time. A different default for missing values, a different unit, a different time zone -- and the model silently degrades.

The structural fix is to compute features through the same code path in both places. Serialise the entire preprocessing pipeline with the model rather than reimplementing it in the serving layer.

## What to version

All four together: training data snapshot, feature pipeline, model artefact, and the code that serves it. Being unable to reproduce a model that is making decisions today is an operational and often a regulatory problem.

## Rollout

Deploy behind a flag. Send a small share of traffic to the new model, compare against the incumbent on live data, and expand only if it holds up. Offline validation is necessary but not sufficient -- production traffic differs from your test set in ways you did not anticipate.

lessons.title: Monitoring, drift and retraining
lessons.content:
## A model that is not monitored has unknown accuracy

Not good accuracy or bad accuracy -- unknown. Performance degrades silently, because nothing errors when predictions get worse.

## What to monitor

**Input distributions.** Track summary statistics per feature and alert on significant shifts. This catches upstream pipeline breakage -- a changed unit, a field that started arriving null -- which is far more common than genuine drift.

**Output distributions.** A sudden change in the rate of positive predictions is a strong signal that something changed, and you see it immediately, without waiting for labels.

**Actual performance, once labels arrive.** This is the real number, but it lags -- sometimes by months, if the outcome takes months to observe. Plan for that lag rather than being surprised by it.

**Prediction latency and error rates.** Ordinary service health, still your responsibility.

## Drift

**Data drift** - the input distribution moves. **Concept drift** - the relationship between inputs and target changes, which is worse because inputs can look entirely normal.

## Retraining

Three strategies:

- **Scheduled** - retrain on a fixed cadence. Simple, predictable, sometimes unnecessary and sometimes too late.
- **Triggered** - retrain when monitoring crosses a threshold. Efficient, requires trustworthy monitoring.
- **Continuous** - retrain constantly. Powerful and easy to get wrong; a feedback loop where the model influences the data it later trains on can drift steadily away from reality.

Start scheduled, move to triggered once you trust your monitoring. And always validate a retrained model against the incumbent before promoting it -- retraining on newer data does not automatically produce a better model.

lessons.title: Project: end-to-end walkthrough
lessons.content:
## The brief

Build a model predicting whether a subscription customer will cancel within 30 days. Available data: account records, monthly usage, support tickets, and billing history.

## Step 1 - frame it

- **Row.** One active subscription on a given date.
- **Label.** Cancelled within the following 30 days.
- **Prediction time.** Features must use only data available on that date.
- **Decision.** Send a retention offer.
- **Costs.** A false positive costs one discount. A false negative costs a customer's remaining lifetime value. They differ by roughly an order of magnitude, which will set the threshold.

## Step 2 - build the dataset

For each customer, sample observation dates. For each, compute features using only prior data and the label using the following 30 days.

**The trap.** Any field written at cancellation time -- cancellation reason, final invoice flag -- is leakage. Audit every column against the prediction date.

## Step 3 - split

Chronologically, and grouped by customer. Train on the earliest period, validate on the next, hold out the most recent as test. Random splitting here would produce a beautiful, meaningless result.

## Step 4 - baseline

A simple rule: flag anyone whose usage dropped more than 50% month over month. Measure precision and recall. This is the number to beat, and it is often better than expected.

## Step 5 - model

Logistic regression first, for interpretability and a sanity check on the features. Then gradient boosting. Compare both against the rule baseline on the validation set.

## Step 6 - threshold

Using the 10:1 cost ratio, choose the threshold that minimises expected cost -- not the one that maximises F1. These are different, and the second is the wrong objective here.

## Step 7 - deploy

Batch scoring nightly is sufficient; retention offers do not need sub-second latency. Version data, pipeline, model and serving code together.

## Step 8 - monitor

Track feature distributions and the daily positive rate immediately. Actual performance can only be measured with a 30-day lag, so build the dashboard to expect that.

## Step 9 - measure the business outcome

Run a holdout group that receives no offer. Without it you cannot distinguish customers the offer saved from customers who were never going to leave -- and that, not the model's AUC, is what the project was for.

courses.description:
A foundations course for people who need to analyse data and be trusted with the conclusion.

It covers the statistics that matter in practice -- distributions, variation, uncertainty and the difference between correlation and causation -- alongside the SQL required to get the data in the first place and the visualisation principles that make a finding legible.

modules.title: Describing data honestly
modules.description: Summary statistics, distributions and the ways averages mislead.

lessons.title: Centre, spread and shape
lessons.content:
## Three numbers, not one

Reporting only an average discards most of what the data says.

**Centre.** The mean is the arithmetic average and is pulled hard by outliers. The median is the middle value and is not. When they differ substantially, the distribution is skewed -- and which one you report changes the story. Income data is the canonical case: mean income and median income can support opposite conclusions from the same dataset.

**Spread.** Standard deviation summarises typical distance from the mean. The interquartile range -- the middle 50% -- is more robust when outliers are present. Two datasets with identical means can behave completely differently, and the spread is what tells you.

**Shape.** Symmetric, skewed, or multi-modal. A bimodal distribution -- two distinct clusters -- makes the average describe a value that almost nobody actually has. This happens constantly with mixed populations, and no summary statistic will reveal it. Only a histogram will.

## Always plot the distribution first

Before computing anything, look at a histogram. Summary statistics are compressions, and every compression loses information. The classic demonstration is a set of datasets with identical means, variances and correlations that look entirely different when plotted -- one is a straight line, one is a circle, one is dominated by a single outlier.

## What to report

For a skewed distribution, report the median and the interquartile range, and say that it is skewed. For a symmetric one, mean and standard deviation are fine. Either way, show the distribution.

lessons.title: Variation and why it matters more than the average
lessons.content:
## Every measurement varies

If conversion rate was 3.1% last week and 3.4% this week, has anything changed? Without knowing how much this metric normally fluctuates, the question is unanswerable -- and acting on the difference is superstition.

## Common-cause and special-cause variation

**Common cause** is the ordinary fluctuation inherent in the process. It is noise. Responding to it makes things worse, because you are adjusting a system in response to randomness.

**Special cause** is a genuine change with an identifiable reason. It is signal, and it warrants investigation.

Distinguishing them is the entire skill. The practical method is to plot the metric over time with bands showing the historical range of normal variation. Points inside the bands are noise; points outside, or sustained runs on one side, are signal.

## Why weekly comparisons mislead

Comparing this week to last week uses two data points, which cannot separate signal from noise. A run chart with twenty weeks of history answers the question honestly and takes no longer to produce.

## Sample size

Small samples produce extreme values by chance. The regions with both the highest and the lowest rates of a rare condition tend to be the least populated ones -- not because of anything about those regions, but because small denominators produce volatile rates.

Any ranking of small groups by a rate is mostly ranking them by sample size. Check the denominator before believing the ordering.

lessons.title: Uncertainty and confidence intervals
lessons.content:
## A point estimate without uncertainty is incomplete

"Conversion is 4.2%" is a measurement of a sample. The underlying rate is not exactly 4.2%, and how far off it might be depends on how much data you have.

## Standard error

The standard error describes how much your estimate would vary if you repeated the measurement. It shrinks with the square root of sample size -- so quadrupling your data halves your uncertainty. That square-root relationship is why doubling a sample helps less than people expect.

## What a 95% confidence interval means

If you repeated the whole procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals constructed this way would contain the true value.

It does **not** mean there is a 95% probability the true value is in this particular interval. That is a different claim requiring different machinery. The distinction sounds pedantic and is not: it is the difference between a statement about the procedure and a statement about this one result.

## Practical use

1. **Report intervals alongside estimates.** "4.2% (95% CI: 3.8-4.6%)" tells the reader how much to trust the number.
2. **Overlapping intervals mean the difference is not established.** If variant A is 4.2% (3.8-4.6) and variant B is 4.4% (4.0-4.8), you have not shown B is better.
3. **Wide intervals mean collect more data**, not "pick the higher number".

## Multiple comparisons

Test twenty things at the 95% level and you expect roughly one false positive by chance alone. This is why dashboards with dozens of metrics always show something "significant" -- and why deciding what you are testing before you look at the data matters so much.

modules.title: Getting the data
modules.description: SQL for real analysis, including the joins and aggregations that go wrong quietly.

lessons.title: SQL for analysis
lessons.content:
## The clauses, in execution order

SQL is written in one order and executed in another, which explains most beginner confusion:

1. `FROM` and `JOIN` - assemble the rows
2. `WHERE` - filter individual rows
3. `GROUP BY` - collapse into groups
4. `HAVING` - filter groups
5. `SELECT` - choose output columns
6. `ORDER BY` / `LIMIT` - sort and truncate

The practical consequence: `WHERE` filters before aggregation and `HAVING` filters after. Filtering out rows before counting is different from filtering out groups after counting, and mixing them up produces wrong answers that look plausible.

## Aggregation

```sql
SELECT category,
       COUNT(*)          AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers,
       SUM(amount)       AS revenue,
       AVG(amount)       AS average_order
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 100
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

Note `COUNT(*)` versus `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)`. Reporting order count when the question was about customers is one of the most common analytical errors, and nothing in the query flags it.

## NULL behaves differently

`NULL` is not a value; it is the absence of one. `NULL = NULL` is not true -- use `IS NULL`. Aggregate functions skip nulls, so `AVG(amount)` over ten rows where three are null divides by seven, not ten. Whether that is what you wanted depends entirely on why those values are missing.

## Window functions

When you need a per-row value computed across a group without collapsing rows:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)
         AS running_total,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)
         AS order_sequence
FROM orders;
```

Running totals, rankings within groups, and period-over-period comparisons all become straightforward. This is the single highest-leverage thing to learn after basic aggregation.

lessons.title: Joins and the mistakes they hide
lessons.content:
## The four joins

- `INNER JOIN` - rows matching in both tables.
- `LEFT JOIN` - all rows from the left, nulls where no match.
- `RIGHT JOIN` - the mirror image, rarely used because rewriting as a left join reads better.
- `FULL OUTER JOIN` - everything from both sides.

## The silent failure: fan-out

Joining a one-row-per-customer table to a many-rows-per-customer table duplicates the customer row once per match. If you then sum a customer-level value, you have multiplied it by the number of matching rows.

```sql
-- Wrong: annual_value is counted once per order
SELECT c.region, SUM(c.annual_value)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.region;
```

This produces a large, confident, wrong number with no error. Aggregate to the right grain first:

```sql
SELECT c.region, SUM(c.annual_value)
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
GROUP BY c.region;
```

## Filtering a left join in the wrong place

```sql
-- Silently becomes an inner join
SELECT c.id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'complete';
```

The `WHERE` clause discards the null rows the left join just produced. Move the condition into the `ON` clause to keep customers with no completed orders.

## The habit that catches both

Check the row count before and after every join. If it changed and you did not intend it to, stop and find out why before writing another line.

lessons.title: Data quality checks that catch real problems
lessons.content:
## Run these before any analysis

Most wrong conclusions come from bad data, not bad statistics.

### 1. Row counts over time

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, COUNT(*)
FROM events GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

A gap or a sudden step change is a pipeline problem, not a business insight. Finding this after presenting the analysis is considerably worse than finding it before.

### 2. Null rates per column

A column that is 3% null historically and 40% null last month means something upstream changed. Analysing it as though nothing happened produces a confident wrong answer.

### 3. Duplicates on the key you assume is unique

```sql
SELECT id, COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

Assumed-unique keys that are not unique cause the fan-out problem from the previous lesson.

### 4. Impossible values

Negative quantities, dates in the future, ages above 150, percentages above 100. These indicate either a data problem or a definition you have misunderstood -- both worth knowing about.

### 5. Referential integrity

Orphaned foreign keys mean rows will silently vanish from inner joins.

## Automate it

A short script running these checks against a new dataset takes an hour to write and will save you from publishing a wrong number at least once. Trust is expensive to rebuild.

modules.title: Communicating findings
modules.description: Visualisation and the reasoning traps that survive good analysis.

lessons.title: Charts that inform rather than impress
lessons.content:
## Match the chart to the question

- **Comparing categories** -> bar chart, sorted by value unless there is a natural order.
- **Change over time** -> line chart, time on the horizontal axis.
- **Relationship between two variables** -> scatter plot.
- **Distribution of one variable** -> histogram or box plot.
- **Part of a whole** -> stacked bar, almost always clearer than a pie chart; pie charts only work with two or three slices.

## The rules that matter

**Start bar charts at zero.** Bar length encodes value, so a truncated axis distorts the comparison. Line charts may use a non-zero axis when showing change, but say so.

**Sort by value.** Alphabetical ordering hides the pattern the chart exists to show.

**Label directly.** Putting labels on the lines beats a legend that forces the reader to look back and forth matching colours.

**Do not encode with colour alone.** Roughly one in twelve men has some colour vision deficiency. Use position, shape or direct labels as well.

**Show uncertainty** where it exists. A bar chart of point estimates implies a precision the data does not support.

## Say what the chart shows

Title the chart with the finding, not the variables. "Revenue fell 18% after the March pricing change" is a title. "Revenue by month" is a caption. The first does the work; the second makes the reader do it.

## Remove everything else

Gridlines, borders, background fills, 3D effects and decorative colour add nothing and cost attention. Every element should be answering the question.

lessons.title: Correlation, causation and confounding
lessons.content:
## Why correlation is not causation

Two variables moving together admits four explanations:

1. A causes B.
2. B causes A.
3. Something else causes both -- a **confounder**.
4. Coincidence, especially with many variables and a small sample.

The data alone cannot distinguish these. Only the design of the study can.

## Confounding, concretely

Ice cream sales correlate with drowning deaths. Neither causes the other; hot weather causes both. The correlation is real, the causal claim is nonsense, and no amount of additional correlational data fixes it.

The practical version: customers who use feature X have higher retention. Does X cause retention, or do already-engaged customers adopt X? Engagement is the confounder, and treating the correlation as causal leads to building more of X for people who will never use it.

## What establishes causation

**Randomised experiment.** Assign treatment at random, and randomisation balances all confounders -- including ones you never thought of. This is why experiments are the gold standard and why the random part is non-negotiable.

**Quasi-experimental methods.** When randomisation is impossible, techniques like difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity can support causal claims under assumptions you must state and defend.

**Controlling for confounders.** Helps only for confounders you measured. Unmeasured confounding is invisible.

## Simpson's paradox

A trend can appear in every subgroup and reverse in the aggregate, when group sizes differ. A treatment can have a higher success rate than the alternative in both mild and severe cases, yet a lower overall rate, because it was used more often on severe cases.

**Always check whether an aggregate holds within subgroups.** If it reverses, the aggregate is the misleading number.

lessons.title: Survivorship bias and other traps
lessons.content:
## Survivorship bias

Analysing only the things that made it through a filter, and generalising to everything.

The canonical example: engineers examining returning aircraft for bullet holes and proposing to armour the areas most frequently hit. The correct conclusion is the opposite -- those are the survivable hits. The planes hit elsewhere did not return to be measured.

The everyday versions:
- Studying only current customers to understand churn. The churned ones are the population you need.
- Studying successful companies for the practices that cause success, without checking whether failed companies did the same things.
- Analysing users who completed onboarding to understand why people drop out.

**The check:** who is missing from this dataset, and were they removed by something related to what I am measuring?

## Selection bias

Your sample is not representative of the population you want to describe. Survey respondents differ systematically from non-respondents -- typically holding stronger opinions. A satisfaction survey answered by 4% of customers measures the satisfaction of people motivated to answer surveys.

## Regression to the mean

Extreme measurements tend to be followed by less extreme ones, purely by statistics. The worst-performing stores improve after an intervention -- and would have improved without it. Without a control group you cannot separate the intervention from the regression, and you will systematically over-credit interventions applied to outliers.

## The habit

Before presenting a finding, ask: who is missing, what else could produce this pattern, and would I have believed the opposite result as readily? The last question catches more errors than the first two.
