modules.title: Delivery pipelines
modules.description: Getting a change from a developer's machine to production safely and repeatedly.

lessons.title: Branching strategies and their costs
lessons.content:
## The trade-off

Every branching strategy trades isolation against integration pain. Longer-lived branches mean less interference day to day and more conflict at merge time.

## Trunk-based development

Everyone commits to one main branch, several times a day. Incomplete work hides behind feature flags. Integration problems surface within hours, when they are small.

Requires: fast, reliable automated tests, and feature flags. Without those it is reckless.

Suits teams deploying daily or more often, which is most product teams.

## Feature branching

Each change gets a branch, reviewed and merged when complete. Familiar and low-ceremony.

The cost grows with branch lifetime. A branch open for three weeks accumulates conflicts and delays feedback until the merge -- exactly when it is most expensive to act on. Keep branches under a few days.

## Release branching

A long-lived branch per release, with fixes cherry-picked across.

Necessary when you genuinely support multiple versions in the field -- installed software, mobile apps with slow adoption. Expensive otherwise: maintaining parallel branches consumes real engineering time.

## Choosing honestly

If you deploy continuously to one production environment, trunk-based with short-lived branches is almost certainly right. Release branching is a response to a constraint -- supporting old versions -- not a default. Teams frequently adopt heavy branching models for release cadences they do not have.

lessons.title: Designing a CI pipeline
lessons.content:
## What the pipeline is for

A pipeline answers one question as fast as possible: *is this change safe to ship?*

Every stage should either increase confidence or be removed.

## Stage ordering

Order by speed, cheapest first, so failures surface early:

1. **Lint and format** - seconds
2. **Unit tests** - a minute or two
3. **Build artefact** - a few minutes
4. **Integration tests** - longer, needs dependencies
5. **Security and dependency scanning** - parallel with the above
6. **Deploy to staging** - automatic
7. **Smoke tests against staging**
8. **Deploy to production** - automatic or gated

## Speed is a feature

A pipeline over roughly ten minutes changes behaviour: people batch changes to avoid waiting, and batched changes are riskier and harder to debug. Optimising the pipeline is optimising the team's ability to work in small increments.

Parallelise independent stages, cache dependencies, and run only affected tests where the tooling supports it.

## Flaky tests are worse than missing tests

A test that fails intermittently teaches the team to re-run rather than investigate. Once that habit forms, real failures get re-run too, and the pipeline has stopped providing information.

Quarantine flaky tests immediately, fix them or delete them. Tolerating them is the costlier option.

## Build once

Produce one artefact and promote that same artefact through environments. Rebuilding per environment means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped, which quietly invalidates everything the pipeline told you.

lessons.title: Deployment strategies and rollback
lessons.content:
## Rolling

Replace instances gradually. Cheapest in infrastructure, but both versions serve traffic simultaneously -- so changes must be backward compatible. Rollback is another slow rolling operation.

## Blue/green

Run two complete environments and switch traffic at once. Rollback is a traffic switch, effectively instant. The cost is running double capacity during the cutover. Choose this when the requirement is *immediate* rollback.

## Canary

Route a small percentage to the new version, watch metrics, promote or roll back automatically. The only strategy that catches failures which appear solely under real production traffic and real data.

Requires good metrics and a defined promotion rule. Without an objective rule you are just deploying slowly.

## The database is the hard part

No deployment strategy handles an incompatible schema change, because the database is shared state that cannot be duplicated cheaply.

Use expand/contract:

1. **Expand** - add the new column, keep the old one. Deploy code writing both.
2. **Migrate** - backfill.
3. **Switch** - deploy code reading the new column.
4. **Contract** - after everything is stable, drop the old column.

Each step is independently reversible. Combining them into one migration produces the deployment that cannot be rolled back at 3am.

## Make rollback boring

The rollback path must be tested, automated and routine. A rollback procedure that is only exercised during incidents will fail during an incident.

modules.title: Containers and infrastructure as code
modules.description: Reproducible environments, from a single image to a whole platform.

lessons.title: Containers, properly
lessons.content:
## The problem they solve

"Works on my machine" is a dependency problem. A container packages the application with its dependencies and filesystem so it runs identically wherever the runtime exists.

Unlike a virtual machine, containers share the host kernel -- which is why they start in milliseconds instead of minutes, and why they provide weaker isolation.

## Writing an image that is not terrible

**Order layers by change frequency.** Dependency installation before application code, so a code change does not invalidate the dependency cache.

**Use multi-stage builds.** Compile in a build stage with full toolchain, copy only the artefact into a minimal runtime stage. Images often shrink by an order of magnitude, which speeds every pull.

**Do not run as root.** Create a user and switch to it. Container escape becomes considerably more valuable to an attacker when the process is root.

**Pin base image versions.** `:latest` means your build is not reproducible and can break without any change on your side.

**Never bake in secrets.** Image layers are permanent and inspectable; a secret added in one layer and removed in the next is still in the image.

## Statelessness

Containers should be disposable. Anything that must survive restart belongs in a volume, a database or object storage. Writing state to the container filesystem produces a system that works until the first restart.

## Orchestration

One container is easy. Dozens across many hosts -- with scheduling, health checks, service discovery, rolling updates and scaling -- is what orchestration platforms exist for. Adopt one when you have that problem, not before; the operational overhead is real and it is not free.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code
lessons.content:
## Why declarative wins

Imperative scripts describe steps. Run them twice and you may get a different result. Declarative configuration describes the desired end state, and the tool computes the difference from reality.

That difference is the whole value: infrastructure becomes reviewable, versioned and reproducible, and you can see what a change will do before it happens.

## Practices that matter

**Everything in version control.** Infrastructure changes get reviewed like code changes, because they are at least as risky.

**Plan before apply.** Always read the plan. "Destroy and recreate" on a database is exactly the kind of thing a plan reveals and an apply does not undo.

**Remote state with locking.** Two engineers applying simultaneously against local state corrupts it. Use a shared backend with locking from day one.

**Modules for repetition, not for everything.** Extract a module when a pattern recurs across environments. Premature abstraction produces modules with twenty parameters that are harder to read than the resources they wrap.

**Separate state per environment.** A blast radius that spans production and staging is a design defect.

## Drift

Someone makes a manual change in the console. Reality diverges from the code, and the next apply either reverts their fix or fails confusingly.

Detect drift on a schedule and treat it as a defect. The underlying fix is usually access control: if people can change production by hand, they will, particularly during incidents.

## Secrets

Never in the code, and be aware that many tools store values in state files in plain text. Use a secrets manager and reference secrets rather than embedding them.

lessons.title: Observability: metrics, logs and traces
lessons.content:
## Monitoring versus observability

Monitoring answers questions you thought of in advance -- is CPU high, is the service up. Observability is being able to answer questions you did not anticipate, from the data the system already emits.

Production failures are mostly the questions you did not anticipate.

## The three signals

**Metrics.** Numeric time series. Cheap to store, fast to query, good for alerting and trends. Poor for explaining a specific request, because aggregation discards the individual.

**Logs.** Discrete events with context. Expensive at volume but essential for detail. Emit **structured** logs -- JSON with consistent fields -- so they can be queried rather than grepped.

**Traces.** The path of one request across services, with timing per hop. The only practical way to find which of fifteen services caused a latency spike.

## Alert on symptoms, not causes

Alert when users are affected: elevated error rate, latency beyond the objective, a queue growing without bound.

Do not page on high CPU. High CPU may be entirely fine. Cause-based alerts produce noise, noise produces ignored pages, and ignored pages produce missed incidents.

## Percentiles, not averages

Average latency hides the tail. If the mean is 200ms and the 99th percentile is 8 seconds, one request in a hundred is unusable -- and at scale that is a large number of people. Track p50, p95 and p99.

## Every alert needs a runbook

An alert that fires at 3am with no documented response wastes the on-call engineer's most expensive hours. If you cannot write down what to do about it, it should not page.

modules.title: Running production
modules.description: Reliability targets, incidents and the review that actually changes something.

lessons.title: SLOs and error budgets
lessons.content:
## Why 100% is the wrong target

Perfect availability is unachievable and pursuing it is economically irrational. Each additional nine costs disproportionately more, and beyond a point users cannot perceive the difference -- their own network is less reliable than your service.

## The vocabulary

- **SLI** - a measured indicator, such as the proportion of requests served successfully under 300ms.
- **SLO** - your internal target for that indicator, such as 99.9% over 30 days.
- **SLA** - a contractual commitment with financial consequences, always set looser than the SLO.

## Error budgets

An SLO of 99.9% permits 0.1% failure -- roughly 43 minutes over 30 days. That is the error budget, and it converts reliability from an argument into a number.

**Budget remaining:** ship features, take risks, deploy on Friday.

**Budget exhausted:** feature work stops, reliability work starts, until the budget recovers.

This is the mechanism's real value. It replaces "engineering wants to ship, operations wants stability" with a shared measurement that both sides agreed on in advance, when nobody was under pressure.

## Choosing a target

Set SLOs from what users actually need, not from what sounds impressive. A batch reporting system does not need 99.99%; a payment path might. Setting every service to the same high target wastes effort where it does not matter and creates alert noise that erodes attention where it does.

lessons.title: Incident response
lessons.content:
## Roles first

In any incident beyond the trivial, name these explicitly and out loud:

- **Incident commander** - coordinates, decides, and does not debug. The most common failure is the commander getting absorbed in the problem and nobody running the incident.
- **Operations lead** - makes the changes.
- **Communications lead** - updates stakeholders so the commander is not interrupted.

## Mitigate before diagnosing

Restore service first. Roll back, fail over, disable the feature flag, scale up. Understanding *why* is important and it is not urgent while users are affected.

The strongest instinct during an incident is to find the root cause. Resist it until service is restored.

## Communicate on a timer

Update on a fixed cadence -- every 30 minutes -- even when the update is "still investigating, no change". Silence is interpreted as absence, and generates interruptions that slow the response.

## Keep a timeline

Someone records what was observed, what was tried, and when. Memory reconstructs incidents inaccurately and confidently. The timeline is the input to the review.

## Declare early

Teams systematically declare incidents too late, hoping the problem resolves itself. Declaring an incident that turns out to be minor costs a little coordination overhead. Not declaring one that turns out to be major costs hours.

lessons.title: Blameless reviews that change something
lessons.content:
## Why blameless

Not for comfort -- for accuracy. If naming what you did leads to blame, people describe events carefully rather than completely, and the review is built on an incomplete account.

The premise: people act reasonably given the information available to them at the time. If the outcome was bad, the system made a bad action look reasonable. Fixing that is possible; making people more careful is not.

## Avoid counterfactual thinking

"They should have checked the config first." That describes a world that did not happen and produces no change. Ask instead: what made not checking the config the reasonable action? Was the check undocumented, slow, or easy to forget under pressure? Those are fixable.

## Structure

1. **Timeline** - what happened, factually, with timestamps.
2. **Impact** - who was affected, how many, for how long.
3. **Contributing factors** - plural. Real incidents have several; "the root cause" is usually an oversimplification that lets you stop looking too early.
4. **What went well** - detection, mitigation, communication. Reinforce what worked.
5. **Action items** - each with an owner and a date.

## The test of a good review

Did it produce action items that are actually completed?

A review generating twenty items that nobody does is worse than one generating two that get done, because it consumed the time and produced the appearance of learning. Prioritise ruthlessly, assign explicitly, and track completion in the same system as feature work.

modules.title: The arithmetic underneath
modules.description: The two numbers that determine whether any marketing activity is worth doing.

lessons.title: Acquisition cost and customer value
lessons.content:
## Two numbers

**Customer acquisition cost (CAC)** - total spend on acquiring customers over a period, divided by the number of customers acquired. Include ad spend, tooling, and the loaded cost of people doing the work. Excluding salaries produces a flattering number that leads to bad decisions.

**Customer lifetime value (LTV)** - the gross margin a customer produces over their relationship with you. Margin, not revenue: a customer generating $1,000 of revenue at 20% margin is worth $200.

## The ratio

LTV divided by CAC is the summary judgement.

- **Below 1** - you lose money on every customer. Growth accelerates the loss.
- **Around 1-2** - marginal. Little room for error.
- **Around 3** - generally healthy.
- **Above 5** - often means you are under-investing and leaving growth unclaimed.

## Payback period matters as much

A good ratio with a two-year payback still consumes cash for two years. A business with limited cash needs a short payback period even at a lower ratio. Model both.

## Segment before deciding

Blended CAC across all channels hides everything useful. One channel at $40 and another at $300 average to a number that describes neither, and the decision -- spend more here, less there -- requires the split.

The same applies to LTV: segments differ enormously, and a channel with high CAC may be entirely justified if it brings the segment with triple the lifetime value.

## Start here

Before optimising a headline or a bid, know these numbers. Most marketing decisions become straightforward once you do, and almost none are decidable without them.

lessons.title: Funnels and where they leak
lessons.content:
## The stages

Awareness, consideration, conversion, retention. The labels matter less than the discipline of measuring the transition rate between each pair.

## Find the leak before optimising anything

If 10,000 people visit, 500 start a trial, 50 convert and 40 stay past month three, the conversion rates are 5%, 10% and 80%.

Doubling traffic doubles everything downstream and is expensive. Improving trial-to-paid from 10% to 15% costs nothing in media and produces the same absolute gain. The largest opportunity is almost always the worst-performing transition, not the top of the funnel -- and it is almost always where less attention is spent.

## Instrument every step

You cannot improve a transition you do not measure. Each stage needs a defined, tracked event. Vague stages produce vague conclusions.

## Cohorts, not aggregates

Aggregate conversion rate mixes people who arrived last week with people who arrived last year, and changes in mix look like changes in performance.

Group users by when they arrived and track each group separately. This is the only way to see whether a change actually improved anything, because it compares like with like.

## Retention is the multiplier

Retention appears at the bottom of the funnel and affects every number above it, because it determines lifetime value and therefore how much you can afford to spend acquiring. A product with weak retention cannot be fixed with marketing spend -- it can only be made to lose money faster.

modules.title: Search and content
modules.description: Building traffic that compounds instead of stopping when spend stops.

lessons.title: Keyword research by intent
lessons.content:
## Intent beats volume

Search queries fall into four intents, and they convert very differently:

- **Informational** - "what is kubernetes". High volume, low immediate commercial value, excellent for building an audience.
- **Navigational** - "aws console login". Someone going somewhere specific. Not winnable unless it is your brand.
- **Commercial investigation** - "best cloud certification for beginners". Actively comparing. High value.
- **Transactional** - "buy aws training course". Ready to act. Highest value, lowest volume, most competition.

A thousand monthly searches with transactional intent is worth more than fifty thousand informational ones. Ranking keyword lists by volume is the most common mistake in search strategy.

## Check what already ranks

Before targeting a keyword, search it. The results tell you what the search engine believes the intent is. If the first page is entirely comparison articles, a product page will not rank there no matter how well optimised -- you are answering a different question than the one being asked.

## Difficulty versus authority

Competitive terms require authority you may not have yet. Newer sites should start with specific, longer queries where the existing results are weak, build authority, then move up.

A realistic first-year strategy is dozens of specific pages, not three competitive ones.

## Cluster, do not scatter

Group related keywords into topics. One thorough page covering a topic and its related questions outperforms five thin pages splitting the same topic and competing with each other -- which is a self-inflicted problem search engines will not resolve for you.

lessons.title: On-page and technical SEO
lessons.content:
## On-page essentials

**Title tag.** The strongest single on-page signal and the headline in search results. Put the primary term near the front. Roughly 60 characters before truncation.

**Meta description.** Not a ranking factor, but it is the ad copy for your result and it drives click-through rate. Write it for a human deciding whether to click.

**One H1**, describing the page, followed by a real H2/H3 hierarchy. Headings are structure, not styling; skipping levels for visual reasons breaks the outline for screen readers as well as crawlers.

**URLs** short, readable, lowercase, hyphen-separated, stable. Changing a URL discards its accumulated authority unless you redirect properly.

**Internal links** with descriptive anchor text. They distribute authority and tell search engines how your content relates. This is the most under-used tactic in most content programmes.

**Image alt text** describing the image. Accessibility first; search visibility follows.

## Technical fundamentals

**Crawlable.** If a crawler cannot reach a page, nothing else matters. Check robots.txt and make sure important pages are not blocked by accident.

**Indexable.** A page with a noindex tag will not appear regardless of quality. Verify it on templates, where a single mistake affects every page using it.

**Canonical URLs.** Filter and sort parameters create many URLs for the same content. Canonical tags consolidate the signals instead of splitting them.

**Sitemap.** Generate it from your live content so it never goes stale.

**Speed and stability.** Slow pages lose users before they lose rankings. Layout that shifts while loading causes mis-taps and is measured directly.

**Mobile.** Indexing is mobile-first. The mobile rendering is the canonical one.

**Structured data** where it accurately describes visible content. Marking up ratings or FAQs that do not appear on the page is a policy violation and risks manual action -- the short-term gain is not worth it.

lessons.title: Content that compounds
lessons.content:
## Why content differs from ads

An ad stops producing the moment you stop paying. A page that ranks keeps producing traffic for years at near-zero marginal cost. That is the entire argument for content, and it only holds if the content actually ranks.

## What ranks

Content that answers the query more completely and more usefully than what currently ranks. That is a high bar and it does not have a shortcut. Thin content produced at volume was viable a decade ago and is not now.

## A working structure

1. **Answer the question in the first paragraph.** Readers arriving from search have a specific question. Making them scroll past an introduction costs you most of them.
2. **Then provide depth** for those who want it.
3. **Use headings** so the page can be scanned.
4. **Include specifics** -- numbers, examples, worked cases. Specificity is what distinguishes useful content from summarised consensus.
5. **Link internally** to related material.

## Update rather than accumulate

Refreshing a page that already ranks is usually higher return than publishing a new one. Rankings drift as competitors update; keeping strong pages current defends traffic you already earned.

Audit quarterly: find pages losing position, update them first.

## Measuring honestly

Traffic is a proxy. What matters is whether the traffic converts. A page attracting 10,000 uninterested visitors is worth less than one attracting 200 who become customers -- and reporting the first number is how content programmes survive without producing results.

lessons.title: Analytics that measure outcomes
lessons.content:
## Measure decisions, not pageviews

Default analytics reports pageviews and sessions, which are inputs rather than outcomes. Define events that correspond to things your business cares about: signup started, signup completed, trial activated, purchase, subscription renewed.

## Name events consistently

Adopt a convention before you start -- `object_action` in lower snake case -- and document every event with its properties. Analytics implementations decay into unusable event lists within a year without this, and cleaning it up afterwards is far more work than doing it once.

## Distinguish micro and macro conversions

Macro conversions are the outcomes you care about: purchase, subscription. Micro conversions are leading indicators: email signup, pricing page view, documentation visit.

Micro conversions arrive sooner and in larger numbers, which makes them useful for fast feedback -- provided you have verified they actually correlate with the macro conversion. Optimising a micro conversion that does not predict revenue is a common and expensive mistake.

## Watch for tracking loss

Ad blockers, privacy settings, consent choices and cookie restrictions all remove data, and not at random. Users blocking trackers differ systematically from those who do not.

Treat analytics as directionally useful rather than exact. When precision matters -- revenue reporting -- use server-side data from your own database, not the analytics tool.

## Sanity-check against the source of truth

If analytics reports 340 purchases and the database says 380, find out why before making decisions from either. Unexplained gaps usually mean the tracking is broken somewhere specific.

lessons.title: Paid acquisition arithmetic
lessons.content:
## The only question

Does a dollar in produce more than a dollar of margin out, within an acceptable payback period? Everything else is detail.

## The chain

Impressions -> clicks (CTR) -> landing page visits -> conversions (CVR) -> customers -> margin.

Cost per acquisition = cost per click divided by conversion rate. A $2 click at 2% conversion is $100 per customer. Halving the click cost and halving the conversion rate leaves you exactly where you started -- which is why optimising one metric in isolation so often produces no change in outcome.

## Where the leverage is

Conversion rate improvements usually beat bid optimisation, because conversion rate multiplies through the whole chain and is not competed away by other bidders.

Message-match is the cheapest available win: the landing page should continue the specific promise of the ad. Sending ad traffic to a generic homepage discards a large share of what you paid for.

## Match structure to intent

**Search** captures existing demand -- someone is already looking. Highest intent, most competitive, usually the best starting point.

**Social and display** create demand among people who were not looking. Lower intent, cheaper clicks, needs stronger creative and a longer measurement window.

**Retargeting** re-engages people who already visited. Cheap and effective, but reported performance is inflated -- many of those people would have returned anyway. Discount retargeting numbers accordingly.

## Test properly

Change one variable, run to a predetermined sample size, and decide at the end. Stopping a test the moment it looks favourable produces a stream of false positives, and it is the single most common way paid programmes convince themselves of things that are not true.

lessons.title: Attribution and its limits
lessons.content:
## The problem

A customer sees a social ad, reads two articles, searches your brand, clicks a paid search ad and converts. Which touchpoint gets credit?

Every answer is a modelling choice, and every model is wrong in a specific direction.

## The models

**Last click.** All credit to the final touchpoint. The default in most tools, and the reason brand search and retargeting look extraordinary while everything that created the demand looks useless.

**First click.** All credit to the first. The opposite bias -- over-credits discovery, ignores what closed.

**Linear.** Equal credit to every touchpoint. Simple, and treats a passing impression as equal to the decisive interaction.

**Time decay.** More credit to touchpoints nearer conversion. Reasonable for short cycles, still discounts early influence.

**Data-driven.** Statistical estimation of incremental contribution. Best available, requires substantial volume, and is still a model.

## What actually establishes causation

Holding out. Turn a channel off for a defined period or a defined region and observe what happens to total conversions.

This is uncomfortable -- it means deliberately not spending -- and it is the only method that answers the real question: *what would have happened anyway?*

Channels that look excellent under last-click attribution frequently show little incremental effect under a holdout, because they were capturing demand that already existed.

## Practical position

Use an attribution model for day-to-day directional decisions, and run periodic holdout tests for the decisions that matter -- budget allocation across channels. Never treat attributed conversions as a measurement of incremental value, because they are not one.
